[arXiv:2409.09722, *Measuring Recency Bias In Sequential Recommendation Systems*](https://arxiv.org/html/2409.09722v1), by Jeonglyul Oh and Sungzoon Cho (2024), introduces HRLI@K: how often the last observed item appears among top-K recommendations. SASRec’s HRLI@10 approaches 0.99 on sparse Amazon datasets. Suppressing that item at scoring time improves reported ranking metrics; this tests the effect of repeated-item recommendations, not an architectural last-item-pooling ablation. The paper does not evaluate exponentially decayed embedding pooling or learned residual fusion.

[arXiv:2609.27201, *A Systematic Benchmark of Explainable Methods for Temporal Attribution in Sequential Recommendation Systems*](https://arxiv.org/html/2609.27201v1), by Akash Pandey and colleagues (2026), benchmarks ten attribution methods using a separately trained, masking-robust probe. GradientSHAP and Integrated Gradients provide the most faithful, robust attributions; raw attention is unreliable, and gradient-weighted attention deteriorates on longer histories. Its temporal attribution analysis concerns explanation faithfulness, not evidence for a decayed-history residual branch.

Neither reference establishes the proposed SASRec mechanism, and the search did not identify a verified paper evaluating that exact combination with last-item and uniform-pooling controls. Its added value remains an experimental hypothesis. Required comparisons would retain identical training and fusion while replacing decayed pooling with the last-item embedding or uniform history mean, alongside plain SASRec and fixed-fusion controls. Those would isolate history aggregation, exponential weighting, and learned gating; the cited papers provide no such ablation results.
